newsitem.title: UK: Frail rand slows demand for EIB Eurorand reopening.
newsitem.headline: Frail rand slows demand for EIB Eurorand reopening.

text.p: South Africa's rickety rand has strongly curbed demand for rand-denominated Eurobonds, and Monday's reopening of the vulnerable sector after almost a four-month dormancy was considered dubious, traders said.

"The rand is still at 4.54 on the dollar and is not really showing any major signs of recovery, and the domestic yield curve changes shape almost on a daily basis," a syndicate manager involved in the underwriting group said.
"I can't see what commercial attraction it has."
The European Investment Bank (EIB) launched a 100 million rand ($22 million) five-year bond via lead manager Hambros bank with a syndicate group of 14 banks.
The paper pays a 14.50-percent coupon
"They're just pushing a high coupon out and hoping they can sell it," one syndicate official close to the deal said.
"Relationship reasons drove us to join the group," another trader said.
A Hambros syndicate manager said the relative stability of the rand and domestic interest rates as well as Euromarket demand supported the transaction.
Added to this, he said coupon payments from the first rand bonds issued last year fell due this month which freed up cash for buyers to reinvest.

A syndicate manager in the group said although the coupon was "a winking light that attracted investors like moths to a candle", he doubted a high coupon on its own would be enough to attract people to buy rand issues given the currency erosion.
He said the current demand for rand was minimal. He also said the size was too small to go to Benelux investors as they had a minimum size requirement of around $60 million.
Another syndicate official in the group said he was not "wildly enthusiastic" about the issue as there was not much rand demand.
But he said the issue was fairly priced compared with other similar-rated supranational issuers with five-year maturities such as the Inter American Development Bank.
"Part of the demand is coming from rand coupon flows on existing paper, which will only result in small sales which explains the relatively small issue size," he said.

The rand slipped to a seven-week low on the dollar last week. It saw prolonged stability on the dollar at around 3.65 after the abolition of the financial rand in March 1995 but slid to an all-time low of 4.58 before recovering some ground. It was trading at 4.5370/20 on the dollar at 1110 GMT.
The last time the Eurorand sector was tapped was by the triple-A rated Deutsche Bank and the World Bank in early July this year.
Deutsche issued a 200 million rand five-year bond that paid a 14.0-percent coupon. The World Bank set a 200 million rand three-year bond paying a 13.625-percent coupon also via Hambros Bank.
Most buyers are Austrian, Benelux and German retail investors who crept cautiously back into rand-denominated paper in early June after the country's currency crisis in February.
At the time, analysts said investors were treading a tight-rope between greed for high-yielding assets and fear of event-risk and further rand depreciation.
Meanwhile, the country continues to pave its way on the international bond markets.
On Friday, South Africa issued a $300 million Yankee bond via lead manager Merrill Lynch following roadshows to nine cities including New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Denver.
The bond pays an 8.375-percent coupon and was launched to yield 195 basis points over equivalent U.S. Treasuries.
South Africa is rated BAA3 by Moody's Investors Service and BB plus by Standard & Poor's Corp.
Meanwhile Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said in a statement on Monday he was delighted with the U.S. response to South Africa's first Yankee bond issue.
